content: The blood levels of metoprolol are significantly increased (several-fold) when administered in certain conditions, which reduces its cardioselectivity. Compared to conventional metoprolol, the plasma levels of metoprolol following administration of metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets exhibit lower peak concentrations, a longer time to reach peak levels, and significantly reduced peak-to-trough variation. After a single daily dose of metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets, the peak plasma levels are approximately one-fourth to one-half of those observed with an equivalent dose of conventional metoprolol, whether administered once daily or in divided doses. At steady state, the average bioavailability of metoprolol from metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets, across a dosage range of 50 to 400 mg once daily, is approximately 77% relative to the corresponding single or divided doses of conventional metoprolol. However, over a 24-hour dosing interval, the β1-blockade is comparable and dose-related. The bioavailability of metoprolol increases with dose in a dose-related, but not directly proportional, manner and is not significantly affected by food when metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets are administered. The pharmacokinetics of metoprolol are similar to those previously described in adults. Factors such as age, gender, race, and ideal body weight do not significantly influence metoprolol pharmacokinetics. The apparent oral clearance (CL/F) of metoprolol increases linearly with body weight. The pharmacokinetics of metoprolol have not been studied in patients under 6 years of age. Nonclinical Toxicology Long-term animal studies have been conducted to assess the carcinogenic potential of metoprolol tartrate. In 2-year studies in rats at oral doses up to 800 mg/kg/day (41 times the daily dose of 200 mg for a 60-kg patient on a mg/m² basis), there was no increase in the incidence of spontaneously occurring benign or malignant neoplasms of any type. The only drug-related histologic changes observed were a mild increase in focal accumulation of foamy macrophages in pulmonary alveoli and a slight increase in biliary hyperplasia. In a 21-month study in Swiss albino mice at oral doses up to 750 mg/kg/day (18 times the daily dose of 200 mg for a 60-kg patient on a mg/m² basis), benign lung tumors (small adenomas) were observed more frequently in female mice receiving the highest dose compared to untreated controls. However, there was no increase in malignant or total (benign plus malignant) lung tumors, nor in the overall incidence of tumors or malignant tumors. A repeat 21-month study in CD-1 mice showed no statistically or biologically significant differences in tumor incidence between treated and control mice of either sex. All genotoxicity tests performed on metoprolol tartrate (including a dominant lethal study in mice, chromosome studies in somatic cells, a Salmonella/mammalian-microsome mutagenicity test, and a nucleus anomaly test in somatic interphase nuclei) and metoprolol succinate (a Salmonella/mammalian-microsome mutagenicity test) were negative. No evidence of impaired fertility due to metoprolol tartrate was observed in a study in rats at doses up to 22 times the daily dose of 200 mg for a 60-kg patient on a mg/m² basis. Clinical Studies In five controlled studies involving healthy subjects, the same daily doses of metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets and immediate-release metoprolol were compared in terms of the extent and duration of β1-blockade. Both formulations were administered in a dose range equivalent to 100–400 mg of immediate-release metoprolol per day. In these studies, metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets were given once daily, while immediate-release metoprolol was administered one to four times daily. A sixth controlled study compared the β1-blocking effects of a 50 mg daily dose of the two formulations. In each study, β1-blockade was measured as the percent change from baseline in exercise heart rate during standardized submaximal exercise tolerance tests at steady state. Metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets, administered once daily, and immediate-release metoprolol, administered one to four times daily, provided comparable total β1-blockade over 24 hours (as measured by the area under the β1-blockade versus time curve) in the dose range of 100–400 mg. At a dosage of 50 mg once daily, metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets produced significantly higher total β1-blockade over 24 hours compared to immediate-release metoprolol. For metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets, the percent reduction in exercise heart rate was relatively stable throughout the entire dosing interval, and the level of β1-blockade increased with increasing doses from 50 to 300 mg daily. The effects at peak and trough (i.e., 24 hours post-dosing) were as follows: 14/9%, 16/10%, 24/14%, 27/22%, and 27/20% reduction in exercise heart rate for doses of 50, 100, 200, 300, and 400 mg metoprolol succinate extended-release tablets once daily, respectively. In contrast, immediate-release metoprolol administered at doses of 50–100 mg once daily produced a significantly larger peak effect on exercise tachycardia, but this effect was not evident at 24 hours. Divided dosing regimens were required for immediate-release metoprolol to maintain consistent β1-blockade over 24 hours.
